title: What is a binary tree: each node has at most 2 children (left child and right child); the topmost node is called root.

s1_definition.oneliner: A binary tree is a hierarchical data structure where every node has at most two children, a left and a right, under a single root.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Node** – the basic unit holding a value and references to its left and right children.
- **Root** – the single topmost node; the entry point into the tree.
- **Leaf** – a node with both children null; it has no descendants.
- **Height** – the length of the longest path from the root to a leaf.
- **Branching limit** – every node has at most two children, which distinguishes a binary tree from a general tree.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the organisational chart at the National Bank of India. The Branch Manager sits at the root. Each manager supervises at most two deputies, a left deputy and a right deputy. Each deputy in turn supervises at most two officers. The officers at the bottom with nobody reporting to them are the leaves. The whole chart is a binary tree because every person has at most two direct reports.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A binary tree is a hierarchical data structure where each node holds a value and has at most two children, a left and a right. The topmost node is the root, nodes with no children are leaves, and the longest root-to-leaf path defines the height. The branching limit of two is what makes binary trees the foundation for BSTs, heaps, expression trees, and Huffman trees.

The key distinction is that a plain binary tree has no ordering rule, so searching it is linear. The real power comes from layering rules on top: a BST enforces left < node < right for O(log n) search, a heap enforces parent-child ordering for O(1) access to the min or max, and self-balancing variants ensure the tree stays compact.

At the National Bank of India, the branch hierarchy is naturally a binary tree. The Branch Manager sits at the root with two deputies, each deputy has two officers, and so on. Traversing this tree with inorder gives a sorted listing of balances, preorder gives a top-down export, and level-order gives a rank-by-rank view for auditing.

The senior insight is that the shape of the tree dictates performance. A balanced tree guarantees O(log n) operations, while a degenerate tree (every node has one child) degrades to a linked list with O(n) operations. This is why production systems use self-balancing trees like AVL or Red-Black.

Remember one sentence: A binary tree is a hierarchy where every node has at most two children, and its power comes from the rules you layer on top of that binary shape.

---

keyPoints: Each node has at most two children (left and right) and the topmost node is the root.
Leaves have both children null; depth is distance from root, height is distance to deepest leaf.
Traversals: inorder (sorted on BST), preorder (clone), postorder (delete), level-order (BFS).
A plain binary tree gives O(n) search; BST rules give O(log n) when balanced.
Special forms: full, complete, perfect, balanced, and degenerate (skewed).
The recursive definition (empty or node with two subtrees) underpins every tree algorithm.
